Ctx<Position> binds the delivery's place in the file; seeking back to it redelivers exactly that message. Position is a context key of the stream file form. Ctx(at): Ctx<Position> binds a FilePosition, and for a delivery it is always FilePosition::Sequence(n): the message's number under its key, counted from one. The value is pinned: a seek to it delivers that same message again, then the rest of the log in order. Stored, it is the checkpoint a later run hands to start_at. The same number travels in the delivery's stream-sequence header (SEQUENCE_HEADER), which each element of a batch carries too. In the manual form the body names FileContext as its context, impl Handle<Order, Reply, (), FileContext>, and reads ctx.context(Position).

Each invoice records the sequence of the order it was made from. Macros Manual examples/file_position_key.rs /// Records each invoice with the sequence of the order it came from, so the next run knows /// where to resume. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), reply)] async fn invoice(order: &Order, Ctx(at): Ctx<Position>) -> Invoiced { tracing::info!(order.id, ?at, "invoiced"); let sequence = match at { FilePosition::Sequence(sequence) => sequence, // A delivery always sits at a sequence; the other forms name places to start or seek to. FilePosition::Beginning | FilePosition::End | FilePosition::Timestamp(_) => 0, }; Invoiced { order: order.id, sequence, } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(invoice); }, ) } examples/manual/file_position_key.rs /// Records each invoice with the sequence of the order it came from, so the next run knows /// where to resume. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order, Invoiced, (), FileContext> for Invoice { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, FileContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Invoiced, HandlerOutcome>> { let at = ctx.context(Position); tracing::info!(order.id, ?at, "invoiced"); let sequence = match at { FilePosition::Sequence(sequence) => sequence, // A delivery always sits at a sequence; the other forms name places to start or // seek to. FilePosition::Beginning | FilePosition::End | FilePosition::Timestamp(_) => 0, }; ready(Ok(Invoiced { order: order.id, sequence, })) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Invoice) .reply() .build(), ); }, ) }

Ctx<SeekHandle> moves the running subscription; what was queued is discarded and a position past the tip is refused. Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle> binds a FileSeeker for the subscription the delivery came from (SeekHandle). Its seek(position) takes a FilePosition, and the next delivery comes from there. Deliveries already queued from the old place are discarded. Seek to a position the file has reached. The sequence the file writes next is the tip, and a seek there succeeds. A sequence further ahead, and an instant later than every message the file holds, are refused with an error. A live subscription then ends, and a replay stays where it was. A position read with Ctx<Position>, the beginning and the tip are always within the file. A seek after the broker has shut down returns an error. A batch body reaches the same handle through FileBatchContext. In the manual form the body names FileContext as its context and reads ctx.context(SeekHandle). A position that has to hold across a restart belongs in start_at.

Job 2 says the jobs up to sequence 4 cannot be processed, so the subscription jumps past job 3. Macros Manual examples/file_seek.rs /// Skips a run of jobs known to fail: the subscription jumps to `resume_at`. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("jobs"), start_at(FilePosition::beginning()))] async fn work(job: &Job, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); let Some(resume_at) = job.resume_at else { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); }; if let Err(error) = seeker.seek(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at)).await { tracing::warn!(job.id, resume_at, %error, "seek refused"); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The worker on the job file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(work); }) } examples/manual/file_seek.rs /// Skips a run of jobs known to fail: the subscription jumps to `resume_at`. struct Work; impl Handle<Job, (), (), FileContext> for Work { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, FileContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { tracing::info!(job.id, "worked"); let Some(resume_at) = job.resume_at else { return Ok(()); }; let seeker = ctx.context(SeekHandle); if let Err(error) = seeker.seek(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at)).await { tracing::warn!(job.id, resume_at, %error, "seek refused"); } Ok(()) } } /// The worker on the job file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("worker", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("jobs"), Work) .start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) .build(), ); }) }

start_at opens a subscription at a position on every startup; a stored sequence is how a service resumes on a stream file. It is a clause of the attribute, start_at(FilePosition::beginning()), or .start_at(position) among the mount-site settings. The mount-site form takes a position the service learns only when it starts, such as a stored checkpoint. A subscription with no start_at opens at the tip. The file keeps no record of how far a service read, because ack and nack report Unsupported on this transport (Acknowledgement). So a service that resumes where it stopped stores the sequence it reached, read with Ctx<Position>, and opens the next run at the first sequence it did not handle. FilePosition::sequence(n) delivers message n itself, so the stored sequence of the last handled message is the one to add one to. The sequence the file writes next, one after its last message, opens the subscription at the tip, so a service that handled every message resumes there. A sequence further ahead stops the service at startup. The position applies on every startup: a subscription that starts at the beginning handles the whole retained file each time the service starts. The guide Resuming and seeking builds a service that stores its sequence and resumes there.

The previous run invoiced the orders up to sequence 3, so this run opens at sequence 4. Macros Manual examples/file_start_at.rs /// Invoices each order once, across restarts. #[subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"))] async fn invoice(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "invoiced"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The service, opened at the first sequence the previous run did not invoice. fn app(file: FileBroker, resume_at: u64) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(invoice.start_at(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at))); }) } examples/manual/file_start_at.rs /// Invoices each order once, across restarts. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order> for Invoice { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "invoiced"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The service, opened at the first sequence the previous run did not invoice. fn app(file: FileBroker, resume_at: u64) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Invoice) .start_at(FilePosition::sequence(resume_at)) .build(), ); }) }

Publish is each form's one policy and its default: replies, slots and lifecycle hooks publish through it with no per-message setting. Each form's prelude names its own policy Publish: FilePublish on a stream file, StdioPublish on a pipe. A service that uses both brokers globs the crate's prelude and writes the two names in full. The policy holds no connection; the runtime pairs it with the connected broker at startup. A registration that names no policy for its reply publishes through Publish, so the bare reply clause needs nothing at the mount site. .out(Ledger, Publish) wires an Out slot, and after_startup(Publish, ..) hands a lifecycle hook a publisher. A reply goes to the stream key its type declares with #[outgoing(name = "receipts")]. A reply type that declares no key is published where the subscriber says, with reply("receipts"). A publish carries a stream key and a payload, and its headers ride inside the payload in an envelope. The policy has no per-message setting, so the publish builder gains no step from this crate and a handler body keeps the plain bound Out<impl Publisher, Marker>. Each publish is written on its own: two publishes of one handler are two separate writes.

The service answers each order with a receipt and writes an audit line through the ledger slot. A file publish appends under the destination's stream key and flushes, so a live subscriber or another reader sees it once the call returns. FilePublish, Publish in file::prelude, pairs into a FilePublisher on the file the broker opened. A publish appends the message under its stream key and flushes it to the file, so the bytes have reached the operating system when the call returns. A live subscription of that key reads the message next, and so does another process that reads the same file. The file is synced to the storage device when the broker shuts down. Publishes into one file go one at a time, across every broker of the process opened on that path. A stream key is a place inside the file, so the destination is the key alone and the path is named once, in FileBroker::new. Under size_limit, the publish that reaches the cap fails with SeaFileError::Publish, and every later publish to that file returns that error at once. A publisher kept from before the shutdown returns SeaFileError::NotConnected. A hook registered with after_startup runs once the subscriptions are open, and a hook that returns an error stops the startup.

The service leaves a record under lifecycle each time it starts. Macros Manual examples/file_publish.rs /// The record a service leaves in the file each time it starts. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "lifecycle")] struct Started { service: String, } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(ship); // Runs once the subscriptions are open; a refused append fails the startup. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |file| { file.message(&Started { service: "shipping".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }); }, ) } examples/manual/file_publish.rs /// The record a service leaves in the file each time it starts. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "lifecycle")] struct Started { service: String, } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( FileBroker::new("/var/lib/shop/orders.ss"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Ship).build()); // Runs once the subscriptions are open; a refused append fails the startup. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |file| { file.message(&Started { service: "shipping".to_owned(), }) .publish() .await }); }, ) }

A stdio publish writes one line to standard output under its stream key; an empty message is refused because a pipe drops empty lines. StdioPublish, Publish in stdio::prelude, pairs into a StdioPublisher. A publish writes one line in the line format, with the message's stream key in its header. The next stage of the pipeline reads that line. This process's own subscriptions do not, because standard output never reaches the same process's standard input; loopback changes that for a test. A payload a text line would change, such as binary data or a payload with a newline, leaves in an envelope and arrives whole (Payloads). A message with no payload and no headers would be an empty line, which the line format drops. So the publisher refuses it with SeaFileError::Invalid, and nothing is written.

The stage answers each word with the same word in capitals, as a line under shouts. Macros Manual examples/stdio_publish.rs /// The line this stage writes for the next one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shouts")] struct Shout { text: String, } /// Answers each word with the same word in capitals. #[subscriber("words", reply)] async fn shout(word: &Word) -> Shout { Shout { text: word.text.to_uppercase(), } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shouter", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(shout).out_retry(Publish).to("words.retry"); }) } examples/manual/stdio_publish.rs /// The line this stage writes for the next one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "shouts")] struct Shout { text: String, } /// Answers each word with the same word in capitals. struct ShoutBack; impl Handle<Word, Shout> for ShoutBack { fn handle( &self, word: &Word, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Shout, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Shout { text: word.text.to_uppercase(), })) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shouter", "0.1.0")).with_broker(StdioBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("words", ShoutBack).reply().build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("words.retry"); }) }

ack and nack report Unsupported on both brokers: nothing records how far a service read, so it resumes from a stored position. A handler settles a delivery as on any broker, with HandlerOutcome::ack or another outcome. The runtime passes the settlement to the transport, which answers AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs a warning naming the subscription. A stream file keeps no record of a reader, and the file client's resumable mode is not implemented. So a subscription opens where its descriptor says on every start, whatever the previous run acknowledged. A service that resumes stores the sequence it reached, read with Ctx<Position>, and opens the next run there with start_at. A pipe has no log to go back to: a line read is gone, whatever the handler answers. What a handler asks for beyond ack still happens, because the runtime does it: retry_after on a stream file, out_retry on a pipe, a cap and a dead-letter key on both.

The service invoices every order the file holds; acknowledged orders are read again on the next start. HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The invoicing service on the file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include(invoice); }) } examples/manual/sea_acknowledgement.rs /// Invoices every order the file holds, on every start. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order> for Invoice { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "invoiced"); // Reported as unsupported: the next start reads this order again. ready(Ok(())) } } /// The invoicing service on the file `main` hands it. fn app(file: FileBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoicing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(file, |b| { b.include( subscriber(FileStream::new("orders"), Invoice) .start_at(FilePosition::beginning()) .build(), ); }) }

dead_letter names the stream key a spent delivery is written to, with its payload, its headers and its delivery count. dead_letter(key) goes beside max_attempts(n). The delivery that reaches the cap is published under that key instead of coming back. It keeps its payload and the headers it arrived with, and its retry count says how many deliveries the message got. On a stream file the key is one more stream inside the same file. On a pipe it is a line under that key, which a downstream stage reads. A service reads the dead letters with a subscription of their own, or a replay when an operator inspects them.

On a pipe a deferred copy goes to the next stage, so the mount site names it with out_retry(Publish).to(key) or the service does not start. out_retry(policy) names the publisher the runtime's deferred copies leave through, and .to(key) names the stream key they go to. Standard output reaches the next process in the pipeline and never this one's standard input. So a copy cannot come back to the stage that deferred it, and the stage says where it goes. Every registration on StdioBroker names it, because a handler may answer retry_after on any delivery. A registration that names none stops the service at startup, with an error that names the subscription and the .to(..) step that fixes it. The copy leaves once the delay is over, and a downstream stage reads it under that key, for example to feed it back to the start of the pipeline. On a stream file the copy needs no destination (retry_after), and out_retry(Publish) there only replaces the publisher. The position is a slot, so .transform(..) runs on the copy; the copy carries the delivery's own bytes, so no codec encodes it.

The stage hands every job it cannot run now to jobs.retry after five seconds. max_attempts caps how many deliveries a message gets, counted in the framework's retry-count header that every copy carries. max_attempts(n) follows include at the mount site; n counts the first delivery too. Neither transport counts redeliveries, so the count is RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, which the runtime writes on every copy. A handler reads the header off its context to know which attempt it runs. Under a cap, an immediate retry travels as a copy too, because the count lives in the header. The delivery that reaches the cap is rejected and no copy follows it. A cap with no dead-letter key beside it writes the spent delivery nowhere. A registration mounted by a bare stream key takes the cap the same way as one mounted by a FileStream. The guide Retries and dead letters caps a service's retries on a stream file and on a pipe.
